issues.legal_issue: A civil court must transfer a possession suit only when the defendant is both a cultivating tenant and entitled to the protection of the tenant-protection legislation; a tenant who wilfully denies the landlord’s title is not entitled to that protection.
material_facts: The suits sought possession of land from defendants who were found to be cultivating tenants.
The courts found that the defendants had wilfully denied the landlord’s title.
The denial was not treated as a bona fide mistake of fact, so the defendants were not entitled to the Act’s benefits.
issues.conclusion: The defendants were disentitled to the Act’s benefits, and the civil court had jurisdiction to try and decide the possession suits without transferring them to the Revenue Divisional Officer.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 6A of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, transfer of a possession suit is required only when the defendant proves both that they are a cultivating tenant and that they are entitled to the Act’s benefits. Section 3(2)(d) denies those benefits to a tenant who wilfully denies the landlord’s title; Explanation I excludes a denial made under a bona fide mistake of fact. The Court approved V. Kuppuswami v. Sri Subramaniaswami Devasthanam and referred to M. S. Ramachandra Sastrigal v. Kuppuswami Vanniar, without needing to decide that case’s proposed additional requirement.

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession: A plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking possession of land from the defendant.
predicates.defendant_is_cultivating_tenant: The defendant cultivated the land as a tenant.
predicates.defendant_wilfully_denied_landlord_title: The defendant deliberately denied the title of the person claiming to be the landlord.

issues.definition: When a possession suit is brought in civil court and the defendant is a cultivating tenant who wilfully denied the landlord’s title, the civil court may try the suit.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court’s need to determine threshold facts that also fall within the revenue authority’s jurisdiction does not change the conditions for transferring a possession suit.
material_facts: The civil court had to assess whether the defendants were cultivating tenants and entitled to the Act’s benefits to decide whether transfer was required.
The defendants’ wilful denial of the landlord’s title meant they were not entitled to those benefits.
issues.conclusion: The civil court’s initial determination of those matters did not affect the interpretation of the transfer requirement or prevent it from trying the suits.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6A of the Madras Cultivating Tenants Protection Act, 1955, requires both cultivating-tenant status and entitlement to the Act’s benefits before a possession suit must be transferred. The Court approved the approach in V. Kuppuswami v. Sri Subramaniaswami Devasthanam and referred to M. S. Ramachandra Sastrigal v. Kuppuswami Vanniar; it held that the civil court’s initial consideration of questions concerning the revenue authority’s jurisdiction does not alter the statutory test.

predicates.civil_suit_for_possession: A plaintiff brought a civil suit seeking possession of land from the defendant.
predicates.civil_court_must_initially_assess_tenant: The civil court had to determine whether the defendant was a cultivating tenant and entitled to tenant protection before deciding whether to transfer the suit.

issues.definition: In a civil possession suit, when the civil court must initially assess tenant status or protection, that factfinding does not change the transfer requirements.
